research_text:
## Research brief

### 1. API and reported value

`java.security.Signature` provides digital-signature generation and verification for authentication and integrity. Its `initVerify(PublicKey)` argument is the public key of the identity whose signature will be verified. The certificate overload instead obtains a public key from the supplied certificate. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Signature.html))

The reported message identifies the **public-key argument to `initVerify`**. The supplied CrySL rule has a `generatedPubkey[publicKey]` requirement, but it does not define the detector message “already reported upstream,” a suppression mechanism, or a Java runtime test for that predicate. The message alone therefore does not establish why the predicate was unsatisfied or what was reported earlier. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Signature.crysl))

### 2. Documented usage and remediation

Oracle documents this sequence: select an algorithm with `getInstance`, initialize for signing with a private key or verification with a public key or certificate, supply the data through `update`, and call `sign` or `verify`. `verify` returns a boolean indicating whether verification succeeded. Invalid keys and incorrect initialization can produce exceptions. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Signature.html))

For certificate-based initialization, the API documents a check on a critical X.509 key-usage extension; it does **not** describe that operation as certificate-path validation. Java separately provides `CertPathValidator` for validating certification paths. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Signature.html))

**Remediation limit:** The cited `Signature` documentation does not prescribe a remediation for this detector’s upstream-report message or require that a verification key have the CrySL `generatedPubkey` provenance fact. The appropriate interpretation of that fact requires detector evidence; the sources do not support choosing a code change from this finding alone. The rule’s seven-algorithm list is also a rule policy, not the full set of Java-supported algorithms. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Signature.crysl))

### 3. Compatibility and migration

- **Persisted and wire signatures:** Oracle states that signature-byte format depends on the underlying scheme. Its standard-names specification distinguishes, for example, DSA signatures encoded as an ASN.1 sequence from `inP1363Format` variants that concatenate raw `r` and `s` values. Changing a scheme, parameters, or encoding can therefore affect verification of existing or exchanged signatures; the sources do not describe the application’s formats or a migration path for them. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Signature.html))
- **Parameters:** `RSASSA-PSS` requires parameters such as the hash, salt length, and mask-generation algorithm to be supplied in a `PSSParameterSpec` before the RSA operation. Compatibility depends on the relevant implementation and parameters. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Platform versions:** Java 8’s mandatory `Signature` list includes `SHA256withRSA`, but not all algorithms required by Java 25. Java 25’s mandatory list includes, among others, specified `RSASSA-PSS` parameters and ECDSA curves. Other availability depends on the implementation and provider; standard support is not itself a security recommendation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/Signature.html?utm_source=openai))

No platform version, provider, existing signature format, or peer requirements were supplied, so a specific compatibility or migration conclusion remains unresolved.

### 4. Matching rule in the supplied CrySL source

The source states the following relevant clauses verbatim: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Signature.crysl))

```text
SPEC java.security.Signature
```

```text
	java.security.PublicKey publicKey;
	java.security.cert.Certificate cert;
```

```text
	i3: initVerify(cert);
	i4: initVerify(publicKey);
```

```text
REQUIRES
	generatedPrivkey[privateKey];
	generatedPubkey[publicKey];
```

The rule names **`java.security.Signature`** in `SPEC`. Its events name `getInstance`, `initSign`, `initVerify`, `update`, `sign`, and `verify`; `getInstance` is a static factory in the Java API, while the other named API operations are instance methods. For the relevant event, the clause specifies **one argument bound to the declared `java.security.PublicKey` variable**. The separate `initVerify(cert)` event binds a declared `Certificate`. The source states the `generatedPubkey[publicKey]` requirement but does not define how a detector establishes that fact or when it emits this particular message. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Signature.crysl))

**A shared method name alone is not the matching clause:** the source supplies both the `Signature` specification and a typed, one-argument event. It does not state that an unrelated receiver’s same-named method matches. The raw file also does not specify detector binding, subtype handling, or a name-only pointcut, so those implementation details cannot be settled from this source alone. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Signature.crysl))

### Direct sources and limits

- CrySL rule, mutable `master` URL: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Signature.crysl` ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Signature.crysl))
- Oracle `Signature` API, Java 26: `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Signature.html` ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Signature.html))
- Oracle standard algorithm names, Java 25: `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html` ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))
- Oracle `Signature` API, Java 8: `https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/Signature.html` ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/Signature.html?utm_source=openai))

The supplied SHA-256 was not independently verified against a pinned copy of the mutable CrySL source. No detector trace or definition of its message was supplied.
